name: 1_recipe_management
summary: Design the data model and build CRUD for recipes (manufacturing, reactions, PI) so they persist in the backend.
description: Recipes are mostly static reference data (e.g. Robotics <- Consumer Electronics + Mechanical Parts, or Tungsten Carbide reaction batches) that need to be entered once and edited occasionally. This goal covers designing a data model flexible enough to represent single-step mineral manufacturing, multi-tier PI chains (P1/P2/P3), and moon-goo reaction chains with batch outputs, plus the backend API and frontend UI to create, edit, and delete recipes. Done when a recipe like the Robotics or Tungsten Carbide examples can be entered, edited, and deleted through the app and persists across restarts.

key_decisions.decision: Recipe data model: `item_categories` (id, name unique) for user-defined item grouping; `items` (id, name unique, category_id FK nullable) - no is_final_product column; `recipes` (id, product_item_id FK to items - not unique, since some products can have multiple recipes, recipe_type enum column ["t1_industry", "t2_industry", "reaction", "pi"], variant_label string nullable, output_quantity int default 1, notes text nullable); `recipe_inputs` (id, recipe_id FK, input_item_id FK, input_quantity int, unique(recipe_id, input_item_id)). One generic schema covers manufacturing, PI, and reaction recipes since all are structurally N inputs -> M output units per run.
key_decisions.rationale: Manufacturing, PI, and reaction recipes are all the same shape (inputs -> output quantity per run), so one schema avoids duplicating three near-identical models. recipe_type is a plain enum (not a table) since the game-mechanic-driven set is small and stable - adding a new type like Science would require new application logic anyway, not just a new row. There is no stored is_final_product flag on items: whether an item may have multiple recipes is fully derived from recipe_type at recipe-creation time (see the API design decision) - T1/PI/reaction products get exactly one recipe (fully-researched blueprints, no variance), while T2 Industry recipes are allowed to stack multiple variants per product because different invention decryptors yield different BPC stats/material requirements. Deriving this from recipe_type instead of storing a flag avoids a field that could drift out of sync with the recipes that actually exist.

key_decisions.decision: API design for 1_recipe_management: item-entry-by-name flow via `POST /items/resolve` (body: list of item names; response: per-name match with {id, name, category_id, category_name} or matched:false) so the recipe-creation UI can show a checkmark for known items and a category picker + create button for unknown ones, without the user ever selecting items from a big dropdown. `POST /items` creates the missing ones (name, category_id only). Once every name in the recipe resolves to an id, `POST /recipes` is called with real ids: product_item_id, recipe_type, variant_label, output_quantity, notes, inputs: [{input_item_id, input_quantity}, ...]; recipe_inputs are always replaced wholesale on edit, never patched row-by-row. `POST /recipes` enforces the multi-recipe rule: allowed if recipe_type is 't2_industry' (regardless of how many T2 recipes already exist for that product), otherwise rejected if any recipe already exists for that product. `GET /recipe-types` serves the recipe type list from a single source-of-truth backend config file (e.g. backend/config/recipe_types.php), which the same POST /recipes validation reads, so adding/renaming a type is a one-file change. Full endpoint set: item-categories (GET list, POST/PATCH/DELETE), recipe-types (GET only, not user-editable), items (GET list with category/name-search filters, GET by id, POST, PATCH, DELETE - delete rejected if referenced by any recipe), items/{id}/recipes (GET - feeds the material_summary multi-recipe dropdown), recipes (GET list filterable by recipe_type, by the product item's category_id, and by a substring search on product name, GET by id including inputs, POST, PATCH, DELETE). No pagination on list endpoints (small reference dataset).
key_decisions.rationale: Typing item names directly (with inline resolve/create for unknowns) is much less friction for the user than pre-populating a full item catalog before every recipe entry. Keeping recipe_inputs nested in the recipe payload (not its own endpoint) matches the one-form-one-save UX and avoids a diffing API. The recipe_type single-source-of-truth file keeps the GET endpoint and the create-recipe validation from drifting apart if types are ever added (e.g. a future 'Science' type).

key_decisions.decision: Frontend pages/navigation for 1_recipe_management: top-level nav with 'Recipes' and 'Categories'. Recipe List page (`/recipes`) shows product name, variant_label, recipe_type, output_quantity, filterable by recipe_type, by the product's item category ('all recipes for Ships'), and by a product-name substring search; row actions Edit/Delete; 'New Recipe' opens the Recipe Form. Recipe Form (`/recipes/new` and `/recipes/{id}/edit`, shared component) has recipe_type dropdown (from GET /recipe-types), product name text input + output_quantity + variant_label + notes, and repeatable input rows (item name text input + quantity, add/remove). Item name resolution against POST /items/resolve is triggered manually via a 'Check Items' button (not automatically on type/blur) - each name then shows a green checkmark + category if matched, or an inline category dropdown + 'Create' button if unmatched. 'Save Recipe' is enabled only once every name has resolved to an id. Categories page (`/categories`) is a simple list of item_categories with inline rename, delete (surfacing the backend's in-use rejection), and a 'New Category' input. No standalone Items page for now - item creation/editing happens inline during recipe entry only.
key_decisions.rationale: Filtering recipes by product category and by name search are the main ways the user will want to browse a growing recipe list (e.g. 'show me all Ship recipes' or searching for a specific item), so these are first-class list filters rather than an afterthought. Manual (button-triggered) name resolution was chosen over auto-resolve-on-type/blur to avoid chatty API calls and flickering partial-match UI while the user is still typing multiple item names; switching to automatic resolution later would be a small, isolated change if desired. Skipping a standalone Items page keeps scope down since inline creation during recipe entry already covers the only item-creation need identified so far - a dedicated browse/edit page can be added later if renaming/deleting items outside recipe context turns out to be needed.
